title: Adding One Gene to a Living Animal
endLine: A transgene tests what one added gene can do inside an animal.

scenes.tts: How do you test what a single gene does inside a living animal? Cells in a dish give a hint, yet a dish is not an embryo. To test one gene in a whole body, add it to an embryo.
scenes.caption: How do you test what a single gene does inside a living animal? Cells in a dish give a hint, yet a dish is not an embryo. To test one gene in a whole body, add it to an embryo.
scenes.visual: Schematic developmental stage (labelled 'schematic') filling most of the frame height: on the left, a translucent fertilized mouse embryo sits beneath a single glowing DNA ribbon (a simple coloured bar, no molecular structure); a faint culture dish behind it fades away as an arrow draws rightward to a schematic adult mouse silhouette with a bold question mark at its center. The glowing ribbon drifts slowly toward the embryo as the opening question is asked.
scenes.narration: How do you test what a single gene does inside a living animal? Cells in a dish give a hint, yet a dish is not an embryo. To test one gene in a whole body, add it to an embryo.

scenes.visual: The carried schematic embryo-to-mouse world dims slightly while the title 'Adding One Gene to a Living Animal' fades in cleanly across the upper frame in high-contrast text; the glowing DNA ribbon keeps drifting gently above the embryo on the left.

scenes.tts: That added DNA is a transgene. First, pick what to add: a gene, a regulatory switch, or a visible label. Next, pronuclear injection delivers that DNA into a fertilized egg. When it joins the germ line, the cells that pass DNA on, offspring can inherit it.
scenes.caption: That added DNA is a transgene. First, pick what to add: a gene, a regulatory switch, or a visible label. Next, pronuclear injection delivers that DNA into a fertilized egg. When it joins the germ line, the cells that pass DNA on, offspring can inherit it.
scenes.visual: Smooth zoom onto the schematic fertilized egg on the left of the carried stage (labelled 'schematic'). The DNA ribbon above it cycles through short labels ('Gene', 'Switch', 'Label') as each is named. A fine glass needle lowers into the egg's pronucleus (labelled 'Pronuclear injection'), releases the glowing ribbon onto a schematic chromosome bar, and withdraws. The egg divides into a small cluster of glowing cells, with a gold-highlighted subset labelled 'Germ line' pulsing as a small offspring silhouette appears beside it.
scenes.narration: That added DNA is a transgene. First, pick what to add: a gene, a regulatory switch, or a visible label. Next, pronuclear injection delivers that DNA into a fertilized egg. When it joins the germ line, the cells that pass DNA on, offspring can inherit it.

scenes.tts: As the transgenic embryo grows, cells read the transgene in two ways. One tests extra or ectopic expression, turning a gene on where it normally stays off. Another builds a reporter line, giving specific cells a visible tag. Adding a gene to an embryo tests what it can do inside a living animal.
scenes.caption: As the transgenic embryo grows, cells read the transgene in two ways. One tests extra or ectopic expression, turning a gene on where it normally stays off. Another builds a reporter line, giving specific cells a visible tag. Adding a gene to an embryo tests what it can do inside a living animal.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls back to the full carried schematic embryo-to-mouse stage (labelled 'schematic'). The glowing embryo develops rightward along the arrow into the schematic mouse silhouette. First, a previously dark organ lights up brightly ('Extra / Ectopic'); next, a single scattered cell type lights up with a green glow ('Reporter line'). The arrow linking embryo to mouse glows steadily as the guiding idea is spoken.
scenes.narration: As the transgenic embryo grows, cells read the transgene in two ways. One tests extra or ectopic expression, turning a gene on where it normally stays off. Another builds a reporter line, giving specific cells a visible tag. Adding a gene to an embryo tests what it can do inside a living animal.

scenes.tts: Now pause and predict. Suppose a reporter mouse has neurons that glow when calcium rises. Each time the mouse turns left, those neurons light up. Does that glowing signal prove that firing those neurons turns the mouse left?
scenes.caption: Now pause and predict. Suppose a reporter mouse has neurons that glow when calcium rises. Each time the mouse turns left, those neurons light up. Does that glowing signal prove that firing those neurons turns the mouse left?
scenes.visual: In the carried schematic mouse on the right (labelled 'schematic'), a small cluster of brain neurons flashes bright green each time a curved arrow sweeps left from the mouse's nose. Above the mouse, a bold high-contrast question appears: 'Does glowing prove cause?' The neuron flash repeats rhythmically with the left-turn arrow.
scenes.narration: Now pause and predict. Suppose a reporter mouse has neurons that glow when calcium rises. Each time the mouse turns left, those neurons light up. Does that glowing signal prove that firing those neurons turns the mouse left?

scenes.visual: The question 'Does glowing prove cause?' remains on screen above the schematic mouse; the brain neurons pulse slowly in sync with the subtle left-turn arrow while a thin horizontal progress bar fills steadily across the bottom of the frame.

scenes.tts: No. A reporter is a voltmeter, not a switch. Watching neurons glow cannot prove they cause the turn. To test cause, drive them yourself with a light-triggered actuator or an electrode. Then watch what the mouse does.
scenes.caption: No. A reporter is a voltmeter, not a switch. Watching neurons glow cannot prove they cause the turn. To test cause, drive them yourself with a light-triggered actuator or an electrode. Then watch what the mouse does.
scenes.visual: On the carried schematic mouse (labelled 'schematic'), the question flips to 'No: watching is not causing.' A small schematic meter icon ('Reporter = voltmeter') fades aside as a beam of light ('Actuator') and a thin probe ('Electrode') aim at the same brain cluster, triggering the neurons directly so the left-turn arrow sweeps cleanly from the mouse.
scenes.narration: No. A reporter is a voltmeter, not a switch. Watching neurons glow cannot prove they cause the turn. To test cause, drive them yourself with a light-triggered actuator or an electrode. Then watch what the mouse does.

scenes.tts: Two more limits keep transgenic results honest. Adding a gene tests what is enough, not what is needed. For necessity, disrupt the gene in a knockout mouse. Also, forcing an effect cannot prove nature used that route, so compare two versions of the same DNA.
scenes.caption: Two more limits keep transgenic results honest. Adding a gene tests what is enough, not what is needed. For necessity, disrupt the gene in a knockout mouse. Also, forcing an effect cannot prove nature used that route, so compare two versions of the same DNA.
scenes.visual: On the carried schematic embryo-to-mouse stage (labelled 'schematic'), two compact comparisons appear in sequence. First, an embryo with an added glowing bar ('Transgene: enough?') pairs beside an embryo with a broken bar ('Knockout: needed?'). Next, the glowing embryo splits briefly into two parallel tracks carrying differently coloured ribbons ('Version A' and 'Version B') leading into two identical mouse silhouettes to isolate the DNA difference.
scenes.narration: Two more limits keep transgenic results honest. Adding a gene tests what is enough, not what is needed. For necessity, disrupt the gene in a knockout mouse. Also, forcing an effect cannot prove nature used that route, so compare two versions of the same DNA.

scenes.tts: With those guards, transgenic mice unlocked major discoveries. In 1991, Koopman and colleagues added a fourteen-kilobase fragment containing S R Y to chromosomally female mouse embryos. Even with no Y chromosome, that single gene was sufficient to make them develop testes.
scenes.caption: With those guards, transgenic mice unlocked major discoveries. In 1991, Koopman and colleagues added a 14-kilobase fragment containing Sry to chromosomally female mouse embryos. Even with no Y chromosome, that single gene was sufficient to make them develop testes.
scenes.visual: Returning to the carried schematic embryo-to-mouse stage (labelled 'schematic'), the left embryo displays two X bars ('XX embryo') with no Y bar. A glowing DNA ribbon labelled 'Sry (1991)' enters the embryo; along the developmental arrow, the schematic mouse's gonad transforms and highlights as testes ('Testes formed').
scenes.narration: With those guards, transgenic mice unlocked major discoveries. In 1991, Koopman and colleagues added a 14-kilobase fragment containing Sry to chromosomally female mouse embryos. Even with no Y chromosome, that single gene was sufficient to make them develop testes.

scenes.tts: In 2002, Anjen Chenn and Christopher Walsh put stabilized beta-catenin in neural progenitors of transgenic mice. Stabilized means the cell cannot break it down, so its signal keeps going. Those brain-building cells kept dividing, and the smooth cortex buckled into folds. The mice did not live past birth, and their folding was unlike primates. So extra divisions can enlarge a cortex, not how primates got theirs.

scenes.visual: On the carried schematic stage (labelled 'schematic'), a glowing ribbon labelled 'β-catenin (2002)' enters the embryo and highlights dividing progenitor dots in the developing mouse brain. The normally smooth cortex outline expands and ripples into folds. A crisp caveat tag ('Not primate folding') appears beside the enlarged schematic brain as the folding slows.

scenes.tts: In 2012, Youngjin Lee, Jeffrey Rothstein and colleagues used reporter mice to label M C T one. The visible tag showed this transporter is concentrated in oligodendrocytes, glia that wrap axons. They then lowered it and watched the neurons. Labeling cells or driving traits, one added gene tests biology inside a living body.

scenes.visual: On the carried schematic stage (labelled 'schematic'), a glowing reporter ribbon labelled 'MCT1 reporter (2012)' enters the embryo and lights up schematic oligodendrocyte wraps along an axon inside the mouse brain. The glow then dims as the label lowers ('MCT1 lowered') while an indicator tracks the wrapped neuron. The full embryo-to-mouse arc gently illuminates for the closing line.
